Getting started

Before your first scan.

Where can I get Cairn?

There is no public release yet. Development builds and screenshots are not signed, notarised public downloads. See availability ↗.

Why might Cairn need Full Disk Access?

macOS restricts access to some app data. Full Disk Access allows certain locations to be measured; it does not mean everything becomes a cleanup candidate. If you choose to grant it, use System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access for the exact Cairn app you trust, then rescan.

What if macOS blocks the app?

Do not disable Gatekeeper or remove security protections to install an unverified copy. Wait for an official signed, notarised release, or follow a specific trusted development-testing process.

Does it clean automatically?

Manual cleanup requires review. Opt-in scheduled rules use approved scopes and Trash only while Cairn is open. AI-tool cleaning is off by default; you can choose approval each time or permit eligible cleanup without a new prompt. macOS CI passed the consent safeguards; live acceptance remains open. Leave these options off for inspection only.

Scans & measurements

A missing result is not zero.

Why does a scan say partial or not measured?

A location may be unreadable, a scan may reach a time limit, or you may have stopped it. A partial size is a lower bound, not the complete folder size. Review the explanation, close relevant tools if requested and run a fresh scan.

Why did moving to Trash not free space?

Trash is still stored on the volume. Moving an item there does not immediately reclaim its space. Emptying it is permanent and changes the recovery options; review the items before taking that separate action.

Why is the receipt different from the selected size?

Selected size describes files. Space freed is based on the available-space increase macOS reports. Snapshots, purgeable data, package-tool behaviour and other activity can make those figures different.

Why is a project missing?

Check the scan coverage and search limits. Hidden tool homes, app bundles, other mounted volumes and some managed tool environments are excluded from project discovery. A folder also needs recognised repository or project evidence.

Why is an item blocked?

It may be protected, in use, changed since the scan, linked outside the allowed scope or not safely rebuildable. Do not work around that check by deleting it manually. Inspect the path and requirement first.

After a cleanup

Stop when the outcome is uncertain.

Can I put something back?

Where supported, Activity & Recovery can offer Put Back for a matching recorded item still in Trash. It cannot reverse a permanent deletion or recover an item after Trash has been emptied. Check an independent backup for those cases.

What should I do after an interrupted action?

Avoid repeating the cleanup. Read the action record and compare it with the actual item and destination. If the app marks an outcome uncertain, investigate before acknowledging it. Do not delete recovery records to clear a warning.

Does an external copy free internal space?

No. Cairn’s supported copy workflow retains the original. A verified copy is a separate fact from removing the source, and neither should be reported as internal space freed without a later capacity reading.

Reporting a problem

Bring the evidence. Keep private details out.

In a development build, Settings → About can prepare a report for you to inspect and copy. The report includes app and macOS versions, Mac model, memory, permissions, scan/cleanup summaries and limited crash details when available.

  1. Describe what you expected and what actually happened.
  2. Note the app version, macOS version and the steps that reproduce it.
  3. Review the generated report and any screenshots yourself.
  4. Remove personal paths, project names, licence keys and any sensitive content before sharing.

A support email address and response-time commitment have not been published. Copy the report for your existing testing contact. Do not post private recovery records in a public issue.
